script.text: Two supertankers may have hit mines near Hormuz. Who really controls the strait?

Iran's Revolutionary Guards say a supertanker carrying over two million barrels of crude hit a naval mine and caught fire on Saturday. They say it used a route Tehran had not approved. Iran named no ship, and the claim is unverified.

The US military disagrees. CENTCOM commander Brad Cooper says the strait is controlled by the US and its regional partners, and is open. CENTCOM says Iranian forces hit another ship, the GFS Pride, with a projectile. Iran says it was a mine.

Maritime security reports count at least five incidents around Hormuz in 48 hours. Cooper also says the US blockade has cost Iran about twenty five billion dollars in oil revenue. That figure is not independently verified.
Will Hormuz be fully open by November? Yes or no?

upload.title: Tankers Hit Near Hormuz: Mines or Missiles? #shorts
upload.description:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) said on October 17 that a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil hit a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire; they said it was on a route not approved by Tehran. The IRGC named no vessel, and the claim could not be independently verified. US Central Command (CENTCOM) rejects Iran's claim of control: commander Adm. Brad Cooper said the strait is controlled by the United States and its regional partners and remains open. CENTCOM says Iranian forces struck the Singapore-flagged GFS Pride with a projectile; the IRGC says it hit a mine. Maritime security reports count at least five incidents involving commercial ships around Hormuz within 48 hours. Cooper also said the US naval blockade has cost Iran an estimated $25 billion in oil revenue; this figure could not be independently verified.
